source.title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
source.authors: Bin Wang; J. Johnston; S. Fusi

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the Platonic representation hypothesis, but its own results concern abstractness within task-trained networks, not similarity between independently trained models.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure pairwise representation alignment across models, scaling with size or capability, cross-modal alignment, or convergence across seeds. Its parallelism-score results describe within-model abstractness. It also cites reports of cross-model convergence from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper derives the optimal hidden representation of task-trained toy networks and measures within-network abstractness (parallelism score). It never compares the representations of independently trained models, seeds, sizes or modalities. Its link to the Platonic hypothesis is an interpretive remark in the Discussion. Its theoretical results are close analogues of convergence: a unique optimal kernel across global minima, and the same population geometry across activation classes. These are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors prove that abstract representations appear at all global minima of multitask-trained nonlinear networks, robust to the activation class and extending to deep and recurrent networks. They attribute this universality to shared task structure and say it aligns with the Platonic representation hypothesis. They offer their model as a tractable tool for studying that hypothesis, but do not test cross-model alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a mathematical theory of task-trained representations; it does not apply the original sources' cross-model comparison methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Theoretical results vary with input geometry and activation-function class; simulations also examine input-output alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: For the specified multitask data, all global minima of the ReLU two-layer loss share an identical hidden representation kernel, though the optimal preactivation measures (unit-level solutions) are not unique.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical analogue of convergent learning: under shared task structure and weight decay, optimal solutions agree at the population-kernel level but not at the unit level.

fits_no_version.finding: Threshold-class and odd-class activations yield the same optimal population kernel up to a global shift, but different single-neuron tuning (modular versus mixed selectivity).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Population geometry can be invariant to architecture details (activation function) under a shared task, while individual unit bases differ.

fits_no_version.finding: Abstract (PS = 1) hidden geometry is derived for whitened and target-aligned inputs, and extended to deep feedforward and recurrent networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised multitask optimization yields abstract population geometry within a network.

record.problems: The theoretical results apply to specified supervised tasks and idealized optimal solutions; they do not compare independently trained models or test scaling with size or capability. Numerical illustrations are mostly presented in figures without reported numerical uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-based training-trajectory and input-alignment plots are not separately cataloged because they report within-network abstractness rather than cross-model convergence.

untested.parts: No comparison of independently trained models; no size or capability sweep; no cross-model alignment metric.
No empirical comparison of networks trained from different initializations. The theoretical claim that all global minima share one kernel is not tested on seed-varied trained networks.
No mapping, stitching, or relative-representation tests between models.
No cross-model comparison of interpretable features or circuits.
No variation of the similarity measure or inputs for cross-model convergence. The input geometry varied changes within-model PS only.
No measured cross-model alignment. The shared-task explanation is argued, not tested against alternatives.

record.verdict_notes: Kept as discusses/T6. The strongest link to the claim is theoretical: kernel uniqueness across minima (Sec. III A) and identical population geometry across activation classes (Sec. IV C). These are not measurements of similarity between trained models. A curator could reclassify the paper as T5 theory bearing on V3/V7 if theoretical arguments count. Rows correctly carry versions none.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of independently trained models, model size or capability sweep, or cross-model distance alignment.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption representations.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test between models.
No comparison of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits across models.
Input geometry is varied, but the study does not test how similarity measures or inputs affect measured cross-model convergence.
The study does not measure whether cross-model alignment is incomplete or plateaus, or compare shared-task explanations with a common-reality explanation of alignment.
